articles.title: What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?
articles.summary: Reaching net zero carbon emissions worldwide is essential to limit global warming, UN scientists say.
articles.body:
Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.

But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.

Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.

Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.

Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.

In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.

It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.

But not all emissions can be eliminated.

So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.

But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.

The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.

This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels .

In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record , which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.

Around 140 countries have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.

It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.

The UK's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen sharply: in 2025 they were 54% lower than in 1990, according to provisional data .

This figure only includes emissions generated within the UK and not from products manufactured abroad and imported.

Successive UK governments have pledged to reach net zero by 2050 and the target was written into law in 2019.

To help achieve this, the current Labour government has committed to:

rapidly increase wind and solar generation to achieve "clean power" by 2030

subsidise electric heat pumps to replace gas boilers

What is the Paris agreement and why does 1.5C matter?

These policies began to be implemented under Sir Keir Starmer's government and have continued to be pursued by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

However, recent decisions have led some environmentalists to question whether the government can still meet its targets:

Approving the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea

Reducing planned investment in heat pumps and carbon capture to pay for defence

Holding a consultation on whether to weaken electric car targets

The chancellor's support for a third runway at Heathrow

In June, the government's independent adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warned that the UK was "not moving fast enough" towards net zero.

However, the Chancellor, John Healey, said in his autumn budget speech that the government remained "unshakably committed" to the goal.

When former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May signed the UK's 2050 net zero target into law in 2019, it passed through parliament with the support of all major parties.

But that political consensus has since fragmented. The term "net zero" is often used by critics to attack environmental targets, which they claim are being put ahead of economic goals.

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "determined" to meet the 2050 deadline, a policy also backed by the Liberal Democrats.

Meanwhile, the Green Party wants net zero "as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050".

These parties argue that it's in the UK's economic interest to move away from fossil fuels, which can be volatile in price. Supplies can also be interrupted by international events like the US-Israel war on Iran .

But the Conservatives and Reform UK want to scrap the UK's net zero target, calling the current plans costly and unachievable.

They argue that, in isolation, the UK's efforts make little difference to climate change, not least because UK emissions are much smaller than those of countries like China and the US.

The SNP has targeted net zero by 2045 for Scotland, while Plaid Cymru has introduced a 2040 deadline in Wales.

There is no single path to net zero, which means there is no fixed price.

But the Climate Change Committee says the policy will require tens of billions of pounds a year by the end of the 2020s, most of which it expects to come from the private sector rather than government spending.

By the early 2040s, the CCC calculates that the savings from moving away from fossil fuels to cleaner, more efficient technologies should outweigh the costs .

Multiple studies have found that, globally, the economic cost of tackling climate change is much smaller than letting warming continue unchecked, which would result in widespread and increasing climate hazards.

However, as with any transition, the costs and benefits can be unequally felt. For example, while there is huge potential for new clean energy jobs, those employed in the oil and gas industry are likely to be negatively affected.

articles.title: LIV Golf is dead ... but it changed golf forever
articles.summary: LIV Golf has officially ceased operations, bringing an end to the most disruptive eras for any major American sport in decades.
articles.body:
LIV Golf was built on a foundation of defiance, greed, "grow the game" platitudes and — most significantly — unfathomable waves of money. But when the money ran dry, the defiance became an unsustainable strategy, the platitudes were as meaningless as a well-struck shot on a driving range.

LIV Golf has officially begun winding down via bankruptcy, bringing an end to the most disruptive era of any major American sport in decades. The final clear-the-course horn sounded in a New Jersey courtroom on Thursday morning after the league's would-be creditor declined to offer LIV a lifeline. The wind-down process designed to address the demands of the league's creditors will begin in the coming days.

BC Partners Credit, which had reached a tentative agreement to fund "LIV 2.0" with up to $300 million, withdrew that offer after LIV was unable to convince enough big-name players to sign on . Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Graeme McDowell and numerous others decided not to follow LIV into its next iteration; Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed had already cut ties after their contracts ran out.

The Financial Times reported that about 30 players had committed to the league's new vision, a global, player-owned golf tour, with another 10 players — including some star names — on the fence about joining. But that apparently wasn't sufficient for BC, which determined the league was no longer a viable operation.

The breakaway golf series, initially funded by Saudi billions, altered the entire trajectory of golf, drawing battle lines between colleagues, injecting billions into the sport, increasing purses, changing the makeups of the Ryder Cup and all four majors, and, eventually, reshaping the PGA Tour's entire schedule. But after Saudi Arabia withdrew its financial backing, LIV Golf simply couldn't continue as an independent operation in the high-stakes, high-cost world it had helped create.

LIV Golf took the sport on a wild, expensive ride, one that fundamentally altered every element of the game. Its impact on golf, as a sport and as an institution, will last long after anyone remembers what a "Range Goat" was, but not in the way its founders intended.

Truthfully, with its rebellious, in-your-face, golf-but-louder origins, LIV Golf was always doomed right from the start. Golf as a pursuit is intensely individual, golf as a sport is overwhelmingly personality driven, but golf as a business is, and has always been, an establishment, risk-averse, lower-case-c conservative operation.

So when LIV Golf — funded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, personified by noted provocateur Greg Norman — thundered into the golf world in 2021, it hit like a bowling ball thrown on a table of pimento cheese sandwiches. Limitless money! Chill attitudes! Live music! So much money! Dance parties! Neon everywhere! And did we mention the money?

The LIV plane almost never made it off the runway. Phil Mickelson gave away the entire game in late 2021, declaring that he was willing to go into business with the "scary motherf******" — a phrase that now lives in golf infamy — of Saudi Arabia to take a bite out of the PGA Tour's imperial dominance of the game. After considerable PR damage control, and more shovelfuls of Saudi riches, LIV began playing tournaments in 2022 with a distinctive roster of players.

LIV's value proposition — sure, stick it to the man, whatever, but mostly the money — attracted many of golf's most notable antagonists, along with known but past-their-prime stars drawn by a payday impossible to achieve anywhere else on earth. Dustin Johnson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Patrick Reed, Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood — each did the same performative "I have no comment" dance before acknowledging that, yes, they would be taking an eight- or nine-figure payday to jump to LIV.

In LIV's earliest days, the breakaway circuit's Saudi backing generated the most heat, with critics pointing to Saudi Arabia's horrific human rights record. Players drew criticism from 9/11 remembrance organizations, and fumbled their justifications for taking Saudi money in cinematic ways. LIV was a prime example of sportswashing, using soft-power initiatives like sports to help scrub the image of the autocratic petrostate.

And for a short while, it worked. With rare exception, LIV didn't exactly draw massive crowds, either in person or on television. But the boundless wealth of the Saudi regime behind LIV was enough to catch the PGA Tour's attention. Then-PGA Tour CEO Jay Monahan and Rory McIlroy, among others, framed the distinction between the two tours in moral terms, between tradition and short-term gain, between legacy and blood money. Lawsuits and accusations between the two tours flew, forcing everyone involved to pick a side.

However, the truth was far more complicated, and the moral stances far more fragile. The Tour realized that it was being drawn into an unsustainable financial arms race, and in June 2023, the PGA Tour and the Saudi PIF announced a cessation of legal hostilities and a "framework agreement" for future cooperation between the two.

The framework agreement caught the entire golf world by surprise. The fact that the framework agreement amounted to absolutely nothing, however, did not. The PGA Tour went ahead and sought outside investment to reduce its potential reliance on the PIF; LIV Golf went ahead and poached several players, most notably then-world No. 3 Jon Rahm, with hints that more defections were soon to come.

Even as LIV continued to make steps toward legitimacy — Koepka had won the 2023 PGA Championship while a member of LIV, and DeChambeau captured the 2024 U.S. Open, and the majors agreed to extend limited invitations to LIV members — the breakaway tour couldn't get traction in the United States. Events in both South Africa and Australia drew significant crowds, suggesting there was an unmet hunger for tournament golf in those nations. But stateside, LIV events dwindled toward irrelevance.

Through 2024 and 2025, some signs of hope emerged for LIV and its advocates. The Official World Golf Rankings agreed to give ranking points to certain LIV players, offering them a pathway back into the majors. And earlier this year, Augusta National chairman Fred Ridley thanked LIV by name in his closing remarks, an indication of the perch that the tour had ascended.

But at the same time, there were troubling signs. Just before the holidays in late 2025, Koepka began pursuing a path back onto the PGA Tour, and Reed followed soon afterward. The Tour offered a one-time-only pathway back for certain notable LIV members — Rahm and DeChambeau in particular — but no other player followed.

Then, in April of this year, the hammer dropped. Just days after the end of the Masters, the PIF announced it would be pulling all funding from LIV, effective at the end of this season. The move came as a total shock to LIV officials, who were forced to scramble for potential investment to keep operating as a leaner, less-flush organization.

And the hits kept coming. Neither Rahm nor DeChambeau seemed publicly thrilled with the state of affairs at LIV. Although DeChambeau got involved with discussions with outside investors, he's also a free agent and untethered contractually to LIV Golf. When the Saudis' wealth vanished, so too did his leverage and his incentive to stay with LIV. The cancellation of one summer tournament under dubious circumstances, the mounting small-scale lawsuits, and the conspicuous lack of investor announcements all combined to darken the clouds over LIV.

Late in July, Cleeks captain Martin Kaymer indicated that there were serious concerns about whether the tournament's season-ending championship would even happen at all. More ominously, the Asian Tour, which had been aligned with LIV, entered into a long-term agreement with the PGA and European tours , effectively cutting LIV out of the international tournament circuit.

Although LIV had sought to employ an open-door policy — its players could play on other tours in addition to their LIV commitments — the other tours didn't reciprocate. The PGA Tour had a longstanding suspension in place for any player who teed it up in a LIV event, and when the DP World Tour also blocked LIV players from its tournaments in October, LIV lost yet another perk for its players.

From there, it was only a matter of time.

So what did LIV Golf bring to the game, and how did LIV change the game?

The circuit's "Golf, But Louder" slogan never really stuck; turns out that most galleries and TV viewers prefer golf tournaments that focus on actual golf, not a Chainsmokers concert or a petting zoo. On a broader scale, LIV's emergence turned golf into a cold, bloody pursuit of money, with tournaments and tours alike touting the massive sizes of their purses … which was good news for the players, not so much for the fans.

More broadly, LIV forced the PGA Tour to take a hard look at how it's done business for the past 50-plus years. The result: an entirely new PGA Tour schedule with two different tracks of players, "champions" and "challengers." The best and most notable players will definitely benefit from this new framework that begins in 2028, the lower-ranked ones, probably not.

On a less-mercenary note, LIV's greatest legacy is that it demonstrated there's interest in golf far beyond the traditional American-European axis. LIV events in the Southern Hemisphere topped six figures in attendance; any tour that's able to meet that need will surely thrive.

LIV Golf enriched players and destroyed reputations, forcing new perspectives on the game at great cost. It's definitive proof that creating a legitimate rival sports league at this point in the industry's growth is effectively impossible. It laid bare the mercenary soul at the heart of the sport. It deprived certain players of prime competitive years on the PGA Tour, but also made those players astronomically wealthy.

For years to come, LIV will be a case study in hubris and ambition, the power of wealth against the power of legacy. In the end, legacy won out … though not before millions were earned, and billions were spent. Golf is quieter now, but forever changed.

articles.title: LIV and Let Die: Rival League Tells Bankruptcy Court It Will Wind Down Operations
articles.summary: LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn't have enough support.
articles.body:
LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn't have enough support.

"The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan," attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. "Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business."

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable "LIV 2.0." But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren't interested.

"BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement. "While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players' last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives , including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O'Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn't going forward.

"Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us," said Scott O'Neil, the CEO of LIV who took over from Greg Norman at the start of 2025.

"LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging — but always rewarding."

LIV suffered a number of setbacks this year, none bigger than losing its source of its money when PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for the league at the conclusion of its fifth season.

The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the commercially known DP World Tour in Europe.

And as the league was trying to pivot to LIV 2.0, European tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.

Kinnings said in an interview with The Scotsman newspaper earlier this week, "But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to 'destroy the DP World Tour.'"

LIV was originally run by Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as "Golf, but louder" with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.

But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.

Key to a new version of LIV was a "critical mass" of players to stick around, and BC Partners extended the Oct. 25 deadline. This was more about names than numbers, ultimately, and it couldn't reach agreement with enough players.

"Ultimately, despite everyone's best efforts, we just couldn't get to the level of combined financial and player support necessary for a viable LIV 2.0 within the required timeline," Williams said.

In the end, LIV held 62 tournaments on every continent golf is played except for South America. It had a feel-good moment in Australia this year when Anthony Kim returned from a 12-year hiatus of addiction to win again. Bryson DeChambeau shot a 58. Joaquin Niemann won seven times.

They are part of a short history, and now have to find a way back.

Brooks Koepka was the first to return. The five-time major champion got out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal in January and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.

Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.
authors: Doug Ferguson and Stephen Whyno, Associated Press

articles.title: LIV Golf bankruptcy hearing: League scraps plans to launch 'LIV 2.0' and 'winding down operations' after losing funding
articles.summary: LIV Golf was unable to secure fresh investment to relaunch in 2027; BC Partners cancelled their plan to potentially finance the circuit into next season, following a mass exodus of high-profile players that included Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia
articles.body:
A lawyer representing the organisation announced the decision in a bankruptcy court hearing on Thursday in New Jersey, ending months of speculation over LIV Golf's future in the men's game.

"The debtors were ultimately unable to bring the key parties to a fully consensual arrangement that would have supported a financially viable LIV 2.0 league," Gibson Dunn partner Matthew Williams, one of LIV's attorneys, said.

"As a result, the debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan. Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind down of their business."

The Financial Times first reported on Wednesday that BC Partners Credit, who had been lined up as potential backers following the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in April, had pulled out of a deal worth more than $300m (£220m).

LIV Golf had been forced to apply for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after the 2026 season, effectively cancelling playing contracts, with three-time champion Jon Rahm among the initial high-profile departures.

Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton, Louis Oosthuizen and Lee Westwood had already confirmed their intentions not to continue with LIV Golf, prior to the confirmation that the circuit would not continue.

In a statement, LIV Golf said: "Since April 2026, the league's leadership team, with the support of its independent directors and advisors, has run a disciplined and thorough process to identify the best, value-maximising path forward for the company and its stakeholders.

"Despite extensive discussions, the relevant parties were ultimately unable to reach a consensual resolution of certain outstanding terms of the transaction contemplated by the Restructuring Support Agreement (RSA). As a result, the RSA has been terminated, and the transaction is not expected to move forward at this time."

'At times challenging but always rewarding' - LIV Golf chief reflects on legacy

The league was originally run by Greg Norman and launched as an Invitational Series in 2022, with the circuit growing over the following seasons to secure Official World Golf Ranking points and player pathways to majors.

Brooks Koepka got out of his deal ahead of the 2026 season and the PGA Tour created a path - with financial penalties - to return, while Patrick Reed chose not to renew his contract and is now set to return to the PGA Tour via his DP World Tour performances.

The DP World Tour said in September that any player who signed with LIV 2.0 would be denied membership on its circuit, with its chief executive Guy Kinnings and Rory McIlroy both saying that LIV Golf was trying to 'destroy the European Tour'.

Only a handful of players, including Brendan Steele and Cameron Tringale, had publicly stated their support for the new format, with BC Partners "disappointed" that "mutually acceptable terms could not be reached" to proceed with the circuit.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said: "LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging - but always rewarding. Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us.

"We created memories that I hope will inspire a new generation of fans to follow, play, and fall in love with this great game.

"Golf has given so much to so many, and my hope is that those entrusted with its future will lead with the generosity, perspective, and shared purpose this extraordinary game deserves."

The end of the road for LIV - what next for its players?

"The writing was on the wall when the Saudis withdrew their funding back in April and the league filed for bankruptcy in September, but there was still a determination - with fresh investment - to persevere with the so-called LIV 2.0.

"Recent weeks have seen a succession of high-profile names announce they wouldn't be committing to this newest version of the league. With BC Partners also no longer proceeding, LIV Golf was left with no other option than to officially wind down the league and liquidate its assets.

"Where does that leave the players? The PGA Tour has been consistent in saying players will have to serve a one-year suspension from the date of their last event - that was in August. That leaves the DP World Tour as the most desirable option for many - with a mid-November deadline to take up membership, if eligible.

"The likes of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia have already said that's where they'll be playing, while veterans like Lee Westwood or Paul Casey could re-join the DP World Tour - following tournament suspensions - due to career money list exemptions. For others, it's more complicated.

"Bryson DeChambeau, who was fully committed to LIV 2.0, has just one year remaining of his option to take up DP World Tour membership, but that's not an option for other past major champions like Cameron Smith or Dustin Johnson.

"Players who would add value to events could be given tournament invites, but even then these are unlikely to be extended to the premiere events. The PGA Tour is also going through its own changes, with it still unclear whether 10 cards will be on offer through the DP World Tour at the end of 2027.

"For many, the pathway back to the top could be a long and tricky one."

articles.title: Penalizan a McIlroy con dos golpes y todos se acuerdan de sus duras críticas a DeChambeau en el British
articles.standfirst: El norirlandés fue penalizado por mejorar la situación de su bola durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship, como el 'Científico' en Royal Birkdale
articles.summary: El norirlandés fue penalizado por mejorar la situación de su bola durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship, como el 'Científico' en Royal Birkdale
articles.body: El destino es a veces caprichoso y Rory McIlroy recibió una penalización de dos golpes durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship este jueves. El único error en la tarjeta del norirlandés fue un doble bogey en el hoyo 12 (par 4) de Yas Links. Sin embargo, posteriormente, este doble bogey se convirtió en un cuádruple bogey, tras recibir una penalización de dos golpes. El campeón del Masters fue penalizado tras considerarse que había infringido la regla 8.1 al presionar con su palo el césped situado detrás de su bola. Había intentado un chip que retrocedió y acto seguido parece que quiso comprobar la profundidad de la bola apoyando el palo justo por delante de la misma. Se considera que mejoró la situación de su bola. El número 2 del mundo se enteró de esta circunstancia después de su ronda, y tras conversar con los oficiales del torneo y sus dos compañeros de partido, Patrick Reed y Eugenio Chacarra, se le impuso una penalización. Rory comentó que le mostraron la acción en un vídeo: “Hice mi primer approach desde la parte baja de la loma, no se elevó, volvió a bajar y rodó hasta un hoyo, y luego, mientras intentaba tantear la posición de la bola, en el primer plano de la cámara se puede ver como un pequeño trozo de hierba alrededor del hoyo baja cuando pongo el palo detrás de la bola. Supongo que el césped no vuelve a su posición original. Obviamente no hay mala intención. Juego según las reglas, intento hacer todo lo posible para no acabar nunca en estas situaciones, pero viendo el vídeo, no tiene muy buena pinta”. McIlroy añadió a su explicación: “Obviamente esa no era mi intención, solo estoy tratando de sentir la posición de la bola, está en el fondo de un hoyo arenoso, estoy tratando de sentir si puedo darle un golpe de 54 grados a la parte posterior de la bola, pero en el proceso, este trozo de césped se ha ido aplastando”. El pasado verano, durante el British Open, Bryson DeChambeau también fue sancionado con dos golpes por mejorar la situación de su bola. No era exactamente el mismo caso, pero el ‘Científico’, que estaba en la pelea por el torneo, defendió su inocencia y Rory fue muy drástico con él: “Sí, creo que no hay duda de que mejoró la línea de su swing. De nuevo, da igual si fue por descuido o intencional (si así fuera lo podrían haber expulsado), creo que no importa. Ojalá haya sido por descuido, pero creo que la penalización de dos golpes estuvo totalmente justificada”.

articles.title: Tiger Woods' Potential PGA Tour Champions Future Discussed By Alker, 'He Wants to Add to His Tally'
articles.summary: Tiger Woods has yet to announce if and when he'll return to professional golf, but it appears the 50-year-old is making progress towards playing the PGA Tour Champions.
articles.body:
Tiger Woods has yet to announce if and when he'll return to professional golf, but it appears the 50-year-old is making progress towards playing the PGA Tour Champions.

Two-time Charles Schwab Cup champion Steven Alker said Woods has had "talk" with other PGA Tour Champions players about Woods joining the circuit.

"This talk, yeah, he seriously wants to come out, there's inside talking," Alker told Golfweek's Todd Kelly (h/t Heavy's Henry DiGennaro ). "He wants to come out and play, and in particular, I think the big events, like the invitationals or Stricker's event and the Furyk event. He's got his buddies who really him to do their events. You got the USGA, you got the U.S. Senior Open. He wants to add to his tally, you know? "I seriously think he'll come out if he gets fit and in the right mind."

Breece Deactivates Twitter After Threats

While there's no timeline for Woods' PGA Tour or Tour Champions' return, he is "expected" to play for the Jupiter Links Golf Club in the Dec. 27 opener of TGL's third season, according to ESPN's Mark Schlabach .

Woods played in just one GL match last season because of back surgery. He hasn't appeared in a PGA Tour event since 2024.

articles.title: Hunter Henry’s practice absence will concern Patriots fans ahead of Packers clash

articles.body:
Hunter Henry hasn't made progress in his injury recovery, presenting question marks for the New England Patriots ahead of their Week 9 matchup this weekend.

Henry has been playing in the NFL since 2016, going through his sixth season with the Patriots. He stands out as one of the better veteran tight ends in the league, helping New England make a deep playoff run to Super Bowl 60 last season.

However, Henry suffered a foot injury during the Patriots' win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 8. It has impacted him enough to the point that he has been absent from practices for two consecutive days , per reporter Mike Reiss.

"TE Hunter Henry, who was limited to eight snaps Sunday after injuring his foot, is absent from practice for the second day in a row," Reiss wrote on Thursday.

What lies ahead for Hunter Henry, Patriots

It is tough news for the Patriots to get regarding Hunter Henry. They await his full recovery from the foot injury, looking to other options if he isn't ready for Week 9.

Henry has settled in as one of Drake Maye's top targets, having reached 85 targets, 60 catches and 650 yards each of the past two seasons. This year, he has caught 29 passes for 326 yards and two touchdowns in a balanced New England attack.

New England has a 5-3 record this season, sitting at second place in the AFC East Division standings. They are above the New York Jets and the Miami Dolphins while trailing the Buffalo Bills. In terms of the conference standings, they are seventh place. They lead over the Cleveland Browns and the Las Vegas Raiders while being under the Cincinnati Bengals and the Kansas City Chiefs.

The Patriots will continue preparations for their upcoming matchup this weekend, being at home. They host the Green Bay Packers in Week 9 as kickoff commences on Nov. 8 at 4:25 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Women's TGL golf explained - how does WTGL work? Format, teams, schedule, scoring and how to watch live on Sky Sports
articles.summary: Five teams of LPGA Tour stars feature in the inaugural WTGL season, including Solheim Cup stars Charley Hull and Lottie Woad; all matches played at a custom-built indoor venue; watch every match exclusively live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
The WTGL follows on from the success of the Tomorrow's Golf League (TGL), founded by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy's TMRW Sports, in partnership with the PGA Tour.

The women's edition of the tech-infused golf league will see LPGA Tour stars feature in a unique team format, with five teams (representing five different cities) of five-player rosters confirmed for the inaugural season.

The season-long competition takes place across November and December at the SoFi Center in Florida, a purpose-built indoor venue, with every shot live and all the players mic'd up for the made-for-TV format.

Both the 2026 and 2027 editions of WTGL will be broadcast exclusively on Sky Sports as part of an expansion of its golf rights, which also includes a further two years of TGL presented by SoFi.

Every match will be exclusively live on Sky Sports Golf , Sky Sports+ or Sky Sports Mix , while repeats will be available the following day on Sky Sports Golf . You can also download the Sky Sports App for news, highlights, scores and reports.

Around 1,500 spectators will be able to fit around TGL's field of play - which is nearly 100 yards long and 50 yards wide, with matches a hybrid of virtual and real-time golf.

Specially created holes start in the virtual world, with players hitting into a giant 64 x 53ft simulator that is powered by Full Swing, although shots are played from areas with real grass, fairway, rough and sand.

Shots from inside 50 yards are from a custom-built short game area inside the SoFi Center, with the 'GreenZone' having a 41-yard turntable that can rotate the green and change angles of the shots required.

Teams play 15 holes of golf each match, divided into two sessions, with nine holes of triples - three against three playing alternate shot - and six holes of head-to-head singles golf.

In the singles format, each of the three players involved in a team play two matches each. Each hole in both sessions is worth one point and the team with the fewest shots on a hole wins the point.

The use of 'The Hammer' increases the value of a hole by one, with each team having three a match to use. If the team throws the Hammer mid-hole and the opposition rejects it, the hole is automatically conceded. The maximum a hole can be worth is three points if both teams throw a Hammer on the same hole and each is accepted.

A shot clock limits teams to 40 seconds to play a shot, while each team has a limited number of timeouts they can use in each match. If tied after 15 holes, overtime is a three-vs-three closest-to-the-pin competition to decide a winner.

All five of the WTGL teams also feature in TGL, which begins its third season on December 27 and is also live on Sky Sports .

Atlanta Drive GC: Nataliya Guseva, Charley Hull, Andrea Lee, Minjee Lee and Yuka Saso

Boston Common Golf: Celine Boutier, Chizzy Iwai, Megan Khang, Lottie Woad and Ina Yoon

Los Angeles Golf Club: Aki Iwai, Alison Lee, Gaby Lopez, Kiara Romero and Michelle Wie West

Motor City Golf Club: Brooke M. Henderson, Jeeno Thitikul, Lexi Thompson, Ruoning Yin and Albane Valenzuela

New York Golf Club: Linn Grant, Danielle Kang, Lydia Ko, Yana Wilson and Rose Zhang

The inaugural season features 10 regular-season matches and each team playing the others in a round-robin format, with the top four then progressing to the semi-finals.

The WTGL standings, like the men's equivalent, use a points-based system that includes two points for a match win and one point for a loss in overtime.

A four-day post-season sees semi-finals played across successive days on December 20 and 21, before the best-of-three finals start a day later to decide the first WTGL champion.

articles.title: Defending champion Hataoka takes a 1-stroke lead after 2 rounds at LPGA Japan
articles.summary: OMITAMA, Japan (AP) — Defending champion Nasa Hataoka eagled the par-5 17th for a back-nine 30 and an 8-under 64 to take a one-stroke lead Friday after two r...
articles.body:
OMITAMA, Japan (AP) — Defending champion Nasa Hataoka eagled the par-5 17th for a back-nine 30 and an 8-under 64 to take a one-stroke lead Friday after two rounds of the LPGA Tour's Toto Japan Classic.

Hataoka, who won in a playoff last year in a rain-shortened tournament, had a 36-hole total of 12-under 132 Friday.

Miyu Yamashita, who won last week's Maybank Championship in Malaysia, pulled her tee shot on the 18th fairway which resulted in her only bogey of the day to shoot 67 and was in second place.

Ana Belac, who became the first Slovenian player on the LPGA Tour in 2021, was tied for third after a 65 with Fuka Suga (67), two strokes behind.

Hataoka, who has five top-10 finishes this season, grew up not far from the Taiheiyo Club Minori Course northeast of Tokyo.

"I don't have a chance to play in front of so many Japanese fans, so I was really happy to be playing so well today," Hataoka said through an interpreter.

The Japan Classic is the last of four tournaments on the LPGA's so-called late-season Asian swing.

Ruoning Yin made a four-foot birdie putt on the 16th hole and won the LPGA Shanghai by one stroke on Oct. 18 to start the swing. In the second tournament a week later in South Korea, Yuri Yoshida won at Pine Beach Golf Links, her first LPGA Tour victory.

articles.title: Bursting firecrackers in Delhi this Diwali? Check timings, restrictions and penalties
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi residents will be allowed to burst certified green firecrackers only on November 7 and 8, between 6am and 7am and 8pm and 10pm, as the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi residents will be allowed to burst certified green firecrackers only on November 7 and 8, between 6am and 7am and 8pm and 10pm, as the city prepares for Diwali amid worsening air quality and a thick layer of smog.The Delhi government has appealed to residents to follow the Supreme Court’s directions on the sale and use of green firecrackers across Delhi-NCR.The district magistrate (East), in an order, said bursting firecrackers outside the prescribed hours would be strictly prohibited, news agency PTI reported.Only green firecrackers certified by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) will be permitted for sale.The firecracker boxes must be properly sealed and carry valid product- and batch-specific QR codes, the order said.Sales will be allowed only at locations designated by Delhi Police. Sale from unauthorised locations and online platforms has been prohibited.The administration has also directed joint enforcement teams comprising district officials and Delhi Police personnel to conduct regular inspections and prevent the sale and use of prohibited firecrackers, PTI reported.The order also prohibits bursting firecrackers within a 300-metre radius of hospitals, nursing homes, health centres, old-age homes, educational institutions and other notified silence zones.Violations may lead to confiscation and penal action under applicable laws and Supreme Court directions.The restrictions come as Delhi’s air quality deteriorates ahead of Diwali.A thick layer of smog engulfed the capital on Friday, with the overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 391 at 9am, placing it in the ‘very poor’ category and close to the ‘severe’ threshold, PTI reported.Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality, while the remaining stations were in the ‘very poor’ category. Rohini recorded the highest AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472.According to the Air Quality Early Warning System, Delhi is likely to record its first ‘severe’ air quality day of the season on Friday, with the situation expected to persist until November 8.Firecracker emissions during the festival could add to the existing pollution load, particularly as the period coincides with the peak stubble-burning season in the National Capital Region.The AQI rose from 389 at 8am to 391 at 9am on Friday. The Central Pollution Control Board classifies an AQI of 301-400 as ‘very poor’ and 401-500 as ‘severe’.The Supreme Court on November 2 permitted the manufacture, sale and bursting of approved green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR around Diwali, subject to specified timings.The court also directed that the complete ban on firecrackers be restored from November 9, PTI reported.Separately, the Supreme Court on Friday said vehicular emissions were a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and stressed the need for immediate, medium- and long-term measures to bring down pollution levels.The court is scheduled to take up the case again on November 16, after the Diwali vacation.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Abu Dhabi Championship: McIlroy storms into contention with career-high 11 birdies in DP World Tour round
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy carded a record-breaking 11-birdie round to move into the mix on day two of the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship; Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Francesco Laporta hold joint lead; watch the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
It is the most birdies McIlroy has made in a single round in his DP World Tour career, with the two-time Masters champion posting a second-round 63 at Yas Links Golf Club to move one shot back of the leaders.

"I did everything well again," McIlroy said. "I drove the ball well. I hit my irons well. I putted a little bit better. I saw a few more putts go in, which is something that I haven't been seeing for the last couple of months.

"I did some work with Brad Faxon last week and feel like I'm in a better spot with it. I definitely saw some encouraging signs on the greens today."

McIlroy added: "I would say I'll be at least two or three behind going into tomorrow, but I'm still in a much better position than I thought I would be. I give myself a great chance, and that's all I can ask for."

Hatton , who carded an opening round 67, getting off to a fast start with back-to-back birdies on holes one and two, before making four consecutive birdies between holes six and nine.

The Englishman took the clubhouse lead off McIlroy with a birdie on the 11th, but he couldn't pull away from Rahm, with a poorly weighted shot on the par-four 16th ultimately costing him a birdie and the lead.

Rahm carded a mixed second-round 67, which included three bogeys and eight birdies, but it could have been lower, with the Spaniard's wayward driving costing him shots on the sixth and 12th.

"[It's been] pretty good play," Rahm said, reflecting on his round. "The only thing to take back would be just a couple of bad tee shots. I'm feeling fairly comfortable otherwise."

Laporta struck a low round 62 on Thursday, but was unable to match that prolific scoring, ending his second round with a two-under 70 after a wayward drive left on the par four 14th saw him concede a double bogey.

Adam Scott continued his flawless week in Abu Dhabi, going bogey-free through 36-holes with a five-under 67.

England's Tommy Fleetwood moved up the standings, carding five consecutive birdies on his front nine before signing for an impressive six-under-par 66.

McIlroy is out to leapfrog Race to Dubai Rankings leader Eugenio Chacarra and put himself in a prime spot to win a record-equalling eighth Order of Merit title heading into next week's DP World Tour Championship.

The Northern Irishman dropped off the pace on Thursday after he was assessed a two-stroke penalty for improving his lie at the par-four 12th, and he started his second round poorly, slicing his drive out of bounds on the first hole before conceding a bogey.

McIlroy shrugged off the early fault, responding immediately with birdies on the second, fourth, seventh and ninth, where he stuffed an approach from 140 yards out to within four feet of the pin.

He continued his impressive scoring on the back nine, making four consecutive birdies between the 10th and 13th holes.

Another blemish would come on the 14th, with McIlroy, who drove the green on the par-four on Friday, opting to lay up. He would then miss the green on approach and card a second bogey.

He quickly recovered, though, birdieing the 15th before closing his remarkable round with consecutive gains on the 17th and 18th.

'I'd rather lose two shots than be called a cheat'

Having had time to reflect on his two-stroke penalty on Thursday, McIlroy spoke again on the matter following his second round and admitted he quickly "made peace" with the incident.

His ball had appeared to roll into a divot on a slope next to the green on the par four 12th hole.

As he addressed his ball, the Northern Irishman appeared to move a piece of grass behind the ball with his wedge and was later assessed a two-stroke penalty for improving his lie.

"Before I left the course, I made peace with it," he said. I didn't dwell on it, or I didn't feel like I did anything wrong. But then at the same time, I said the video didn't look good.

"I just never wanted the perception, people feeling like I got away with something. I wouldn't want that sitting with me.

"I'd much rather be two shots worse off than be called a cheat. That's what I did, and I made peace with it.

"I went out today [Friday] and it wasn't playing on my mind. I had a clear conscience, and I could just go and play."

articles.title: Abu Dhabi Championship: McIlroy shoots 63 to move into contention on day two
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy recovers from the setback of being penalised two shots in his opening round at the Abu Dhabi Championship by firing 11 birdies in a nine-under-par 63 in round two on Friday.
articles.body:
Abu Dhabi Championship second-round leaderboard

12 J Rahm (Spa), T Hatton (Eng), F Laporta (Ita); -11 S Bairstow (Eng), R McIlroy (NI), A Meronk (Pol), M Jordan (Eng); -10 B Wiesberger (Aut), D Puig (Spa); -9 M Elvira (Spa), A Scott (Aus); -8 D Hillier (NZ), E Ferguson (Sco), T Fleetwood (Eng)

Selected others: -7 M Wallace (Eng); -6 A Rai (Eng); -3 E Chacarro (Spa); +1 P Reed (US)

Rory McIlroy posted 11 birdies in a nine-under-par second-round 63 at the Abu Dhabi Championship to move within one shot of the lead.

The 37-year-old put the setback of the two-shot penalty he received on Thursday behind him as he completed the best round of the day to reach 11 under overall.

Spain's Jon Rahm, England's Tyrell Hatton and Italy's Francesco Laporta share the lead at 12 under, while McIlroy is part of a four-strong group that includes the English duo of Sam Bairstow and Matthew Jordan, plus Poland's Adrian Meronk.

Laporta held the first-round lead at 10 under, but has been joined at the top of the leaderboard by Rahm and Hatton, who both outscored him on Friday.

McIlroy had been handed his sanction for improving his lie during the opening round and as a result finished day one on two under par - eight shots back.

The six-time major winner was penalised after pressing down on the grass behind his ball with his club before hitting a chip on the par-four 12th at Yas Links.

McIlroy began his second round with a bogey at the first but bounced back by picking up shots at the second, fourth and seventh holes.

The back-to-back Masters champion then stormed up the leaderboard with five consecutive birdies from holes nine to 13.

A dropped shot at the 14th proved to be only a temporary blip as he recorded two further birdies on the 17th and 18th holes to cap a scintillating round.

It is the first time in his career he has made 11 birdies in a single round of a DP World Tour event.

After his round, McIlroy said he had "made peace" with the circumstances around the two-shot penalty and felt free to go out and post a good score.

"I went out today, like it wasn't playing on my mind. I had a clear conscience, and I could just go and play," he said.

"It wasn't like I got off to the greatest of starts, but then obviously I got it going.

"I did everything well again. I drove the ball well. I hit my irons well. I putted a little bit better. I saw a few more putts go in, which is something that I haven't been seeing for the last couple of months.

"I definitely saw some encouraging signs on the greens today."

McIlroy is chasing a fifth Race to Dubai title in a row and a record-equalling eighth in total, which would draw him level with Scotland's Colin Montgomerie.

McIlroy went into the Abu Dhabi tournament in third position in the standings, behind leader Eugenio Chacarra and second-placed Patrick Reed.

American Reed was the long-time Race to Dubai leader after his Rolex Series victory in Dubai and win in Qatar but was recently overtaken as Spaniard Chacarra claimed a third triumph of the season at the DP World India Championship.

Chacarra shot a second-round 71 on Friday to sit well down the field on three under, while Reed registered the same score to lie further back on one over.

The top 70 available players from the Race to Dubai rankings are competing in Abu Dhabi, with the top 50 progressing to next week's season-ending DP World Tour Championship in Dubai.

articles.title: LIV Golf: What lies ahead for Bryson DeChambeau and co and what's next for the failed breakaway league?
articles.summary: Bryson DeChambeau has lost his DP World Tour exemption for 2028 and 2029; the two-time major winner can still take up membership for 2027 season, but must state his intention to do so by November 15 deadline; What next too for LIV Golf and other star players after league's dissolution?
articles.body:
The future of DeChambeau - who has lost his DP World Tour exemption for 2028 and 2029 - is one of a number of questions still to be answered after LIV Golf announced this week that it will enter liquidation.

How has it got to this point for the breakaway league that threw huge sums of money at the sport and played the role of major disruptor when it entered onto the scene five years ago? And what's next for DeChambeau and other star names assessing their next steps with the demise of the proposed LIV 2.0?

LIV Golf's attempt to establish itself as a permanent rival to the PGA Tour has effectively come to an end as, on November 5, the league confirmed it would begin an orderly wind-down of its operations after failing to secure the financial backing needed to continue.

"The writing was on the wall from April of this year, when the Saudi Public Investment Fund [PIF] announced they'd be pulling the plug, that they wouldn't be investing in the tour any longer," says Sky Sports News' Jamie Weir.

"They came in with the intent to change the face of men's professional golf. £6bn of Saudi money has been pumped into it over the last four years and most of it has gone down the drain.

"You would have to say that, because they haven't made much of an impact - certainly not in terms of viewing figures."

LIV subsequently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, with investment firm BC Partners emerging as a potential new backer, proposing a deal worth around $300m to help launch LIV 2.0.

However, that rescue plan collapsed amid a mass player exodus and the proposed investment was withdrawn. LIV has now moved towards liquidation rather than attempting to launch another season.

"LIV Golf's eventual demise throws into doubt what the future holds for many, but no one more so than the league's biggest star and most vociferous advocate," says Weir.

"Love him or hate him, DeChambeau has star factor. He puts bums on seats, he commands eyeballs and column inches. He is box office.

"Until the bitter end, he believed fully in LIV 2.0, the phoenix from the flames version of the beleaguered and controversial golf tour.

"One source told me that in a meeting of LIV's 13 team captains in August, when the end was seemingly nigh, DeChambeau was the only one who still passionately felt there was a way forward and attempted to win over the other 12, who were resigned to LIV's fate. No one was willing to take that leap into the unknown with him.

"By virtue of winning the 2024 US Open at Pinehurst, DeChambeau earned a five-year exemption on the DP World Tour. However, the rules state that for every year a major champion fails to take up his membership, they lose a year off the end of this period.

"In other words, having failed to take up DP World Tour membership in 2025 and 2026, DeChambeau lost his exemption for 2028 and 2029.

"That means he does still have the option of taking up membership for the 2027 season, but must inform the Tour of his intention to do so by its deadline of November 15."

Could DeChambeau follow Reed or consider retirement?

"Taking up the exemption would give DeChambeau the opportunity to 'do a Patrick Reed'. In January, Reed took the decision to leave LIV and play his 2026 season solely on the DP World Tour.

"His strong performances (two wins early in the year in Dubai and Qatar, plus runner-up finishes in Bahrain and Ireland) mean the 2018 Masters champion currently sits second on the Race to Dubai standings, and will therefore earn one of 10 PGA Tour cards for 2027.

"However, with the PGA Tour undergoing its own restructure, and moving to a far more cut-throat, meritocratic model in 2028, it is as yet undecided as to whether there will still be 10 cards on offer to DP World Tour members 12 months from now.

"Indications are there will still be some, and that the carrot will remain in place, but the exact number has yet to be specified. So the pathway back to the PGA Tour for DeChambeau, and indeed for many, could be trickier than it has proved to be for Reed.

"Which leaves us with another alternative. The nuclear option, whereby DeChambeau, at the age of just 33, decides he's done with professional golf.

"This is a character who can only be described as one of a kind, with a penchant for always wanting to be the centre of attention.

"Remember, this is the man who threatened to walk out mid-tournament of this year's Open when handed a two-shot penalty for improving his stance.

"A bombshell retirement announcement can certainly not be ruled out, especially given the adulation and gratification he derives from what would appear to be his true passion, content creation.

"DeChambeau has an army of adoring fans; three million plus subscribe to his YouTube channel, where his admittedly captivating and impeccably well-produced videos have approached 750m views.

"There is always the possibility he continues with this, an avenue which clearly brings him great enjoyment, while playing just the four majors and no other professional tournaments. He is exempt for the next 12 major championships, taking him through to The Open in 2029, and beyond that, for the US Open until 2034.

"More recent quotes from DeChambeau would suggest, though, that a return to the top level is still his desire. In August, he said: 'Personally, I'd love to be able to play events on the PGA Tour. I think that's best for golf. I'd love that. It's not an either/or mentality. It's 'can we do both?' I think that's where everybody wants to be.'

"Whether it's delighting his cult following in the content creation space, ruffling feathers in some way, shape or form on one of golf's two biggest tours or contending for major championships, we certainly haven't seen the last of Bryson Aldrich DeChambeau.

"Even if it may not be the case, he'll no doubt believe he holds all the cards. We now have to wait for him to play them."

Former European Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley believes LIV Golf was destined to fail from the very start, following the news of the former PIF-backed venture being wound down.

Speaking on RTÉ's Morning Ireland , McGinley said: "I think it was based on bad fundamentals, I think that was the main thing.

"LIV had an idea that team events was going to work in an individual sport that golf is. They also took on the might of America, but as Warren Buffet would say in business terms, 'don't bet against Uncle Sam'.

"They went head-to-head, toe-to-toe with corporate America, which is the backbone of the PGA Tour, and came out on the wrong side of that. They were incredibly strong and able to move the financial needle in order to stand toe-to-toe with the Saudis.

"Ultimately, LIV wasn't thought through well and it wasn't a great idea. It was a flawed business model with really bad advice that the Saudis got in terms of the power that they were taking on."

The Golf Channel 's Brandel Chamblee specifically pointed to October 12, and the DP World Tour's announcement that players who signed with LIV 2.0 wouldn't be allowed to play on the tour, as the beginning of the end for LIV.

Chamblee said: "When Guy Kennings [DP World Tour CEO] said what he did, that was the death knell strategically.

"He was saying, 'look, you don't get to have your cake and eat it too'. That is the big, significant moment in in ending LIV Golf.

"We're going to say it's November 5 when LIV died. But really, LIV died on October 12."

McGinley added to Sky Sports: "To be quite blunt and frank, they [LIV players] filled their pockets with money and had made enough they needed to make and now was an opportunity to come back in, join the ecosystem again, get back on the gravy train of the DP World Tour, along with the PGA Tour, back inside the fold and move forward.

"It's nothing more, nothing less than that.

"When it became about money and 'is this product [LIV 2.0] believable to go forward and make money?' they obviously decided no and in their heart of hearts they knew that was the case."

Mickelson was arguably the LIV's most significant signing in its early days. The six-time major champion's decision to join in 2022 was a major statement of intent.

Four years on, his future is one of the biggest question marks off the back of the league's collapse.

At 56 years old, Mickelson's best is long behind him - even when considering his remarkable 2021 PGA Championship success - and, thus far, he has not signalled his intent with regards to any future plans.

His relationship with the PGA Tour has been particularly complicated, given his involvement in the original push for LIV and the legal disputes that followed.

One possibility is that Mickelson focuses only on playing at major championships, where he can still compete through his existing exemptions where applicable.

Further complicating his future in the game, however, are allegations of misconduct made against him, with golf publication Skratch alleged earlier this year that he's is no longer welcome at three California golf clubs because of inappropriate behaviour towards women.

Mickelson denies the allegations, with his representatives calling the piece an "anonymously sourced drive-by shooting".

Mickelson played only one LIV tournament this year, in South Africa in March, missing the rest of their schedule to prioritise "a family health matter".

What about other LIV players? Will they be welcomed back?

"This is the great question. What happens to all those players? And it's complicated," says Weir.

"As far as the PGA Tour are concerned, they have been very consistent. They have said you need to serve a one-year suspension from your last LIV event before you're eligible to play in the PGA Tour again.

"That means it won't be until August 2027 that any of these players are eligible to even play on the PGA Tour, as there won't be the same loophole, the same olive branch that was extended in January of this year to four specific players: Brooks Koepka, Bryson DeChambeau, John Ram, and Cameron Smith, which was essentially 'come back and all is forgiven'.

"Koepka was the only one who took that offer. The other three are probably ruing that decision now.

"What that means is that the DP World Tour is now the most desirable option for a lot of these players. They have until November 15 to take up DP World Tour membership, if eligible.

"In the cases of Rahm and Tyrell Hatton, they never gave up their membership. So that's all hunky dory.

"The likes of veterans Lee Westwood and Paul Casey, they haven't stated their intention yet, but they have career money list exemptions, so they could rejoin the DP World Tour.

"For other major champions, the likes of Smith, Phil Mickelson and Dustin Johnson, that door is closed.

"It means they're going to have to rely on invites to events on the DP World Tour, and even if they get invites, they will have to add value to that event. And it's not going to be to the premier events.

"It's going to be a long and very tricky road back to the top."

As things stand, LIV Golf as we know it, is heading for the end, with its assets being prepared for liquidation.

LIV's creditors committee will meet on November 20 and another hearing in the bankruptcy case is scheduled for November 24.

That does not necessarily mean, however, that the concept of a breakaway golf competition will disappear forever.

Much like the proposed Super League in football in 2021, the threat of another attempted coup could loom large indefinitely.

LIV demonstrated that there was an appetite, among other things, for some sort of team golf style events, a more favourable schedule, more international tournaments and bigger prize funds, which has forced the PGA Tour to reconsider aspects of its own business model.

There could still be opportunities for investors to purchase LIV's remaining assets, trademarks or other commercial interests.

However, recreating the competition would require significant financial backing and the commitment of leading players. But those burnt by its ultimate collapse on this occasion will surely be reticent to attach themselves to the brand once more.

And without the players, finding investors willing to take on the financial risk will be nigh on impossible.

articles.title: LIV Golf: Lee Westwood worried for DP World Tour's future after rival tour's collapse
articles.summary: Former world number one Lee Westwood expects the PGA Tour to "play hardball" with its European counterparts following the demise of LIV.
articles.body:
Lee Westwood is worried about the future of the Europe-based DP World Tour following the collapse of LIV Golf.

The 53-year-old Englishman was among the high-profile players lured to LIV when the controversial Saudi-backed breakaway tour began in 2022.

LIV this week confirmed its intention to wind down operations after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) withdrew its financial support and potential new investors pulled out of a deal to back LIV continuing in a new form.

LIV's collapse is a boost for the USA's PGA Tour and Westwood's former Ryder Cup team-mate Rory McIlroy agrees with DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings' assertion that LIV aimed to "destroy" their European rivals.

However, Westwood questions how strong a position the DP World Tour now finds itself in.

The former world number one expects the PGA Tour boss to "play hardball" with its European counterparts and suggested that Europe's top players may be better off playing on the Korn Ferry Tour, the US feeder circuit to the PGA Tour.

"LIV going out of business, some people will be disappointed and it might not be people that you immediately think of," Westwood told BBC Sport.

"The European tour, I'm not sure it's such a big win for them."

Although LIV players were banned from the PGA Tour, they could still play in some DP World Tour events, which Westwood felt gave them some "leverage" but "now LIV's out [of] the way, they've lost that".

However, in July the American and European tours extended their strategic alliance, which includes Annual Investment Payments (AIPs). Last year that figure was £59m.

The PGA Tour also gives tour cards to the top 10 finishers on the DP World Tour who are not already members, but Westwood believes "there are a lot of questions still to be answered" regarding the new terms of their alliance.

"If [the DP World Tour] want to continue having the PGA Tour bankrolling them, there are going to be some big asks from the PGA Tour," Westwood added.

"If I was [chief executive] Brian Rolapp running the PGA Tour, I would be playing hardball and making a lot of demands of the European tour if they expected me to finance it going forward."

A spokesperson for the DP World Tour told BBC Sport that it remains in "a robust and healthy position with strong cash reserves".

"Such progress is remarkable coming, as it did, against the backdrop of havoc in the global golf market caused by an entity which took prize funds to an artificially high level and on the back of what has been proven to be an entirely unsustainable economic model operating within a false economy," a spokesperson said.

"We look forward to the 2027 season and beyond for many reasons - not least because the player interest in competing on our Tour has never been stronger."

Westwood did not commit to LIV 2.0, as it was known, and is currently "unemployed" as he considers his future but would have to serve a 10-tournament suspension if he opted to rejoin the DP World Tour.

The PGA Tour describes the Korn Ferry Tour as its "premier pathway", with 20 cards on offer, and announced a new competitive structure in June with a Championship Series and a lower-tier Challenger Series.

The Championship Series will feature a "limited series" of events co-sanctioned by the DP World Tour, which has so far announced the prize fund for just one event in 2027 – the Hero Dubai Desert Classic in January.

"The PGA Tour put this 'plan for the future' in place and the DP World Tour is not mentioned a whole lot in that," said Westwood.

"[Rolapp has] already said that the Korn Ferry Tour is going to be the main route into the PGA Tour, which makes me think 'what's going to happen to the DP World Tour?'

"I don't think the DP World Tour has announced any prize funds for next year, which is slightly worrying, and what will prize funds look like from 2028 onwards? There are a lot of questions still to be answered in that strategic alliance partnership."

articles.title: Rahm comparte el liderato en Abu Dabi con su 'bestie', McIlroy bate récords y Chacarra se queda a medias
articles.standfirst: El 'León de Barrika' se pone al frente del Abu Dhabi Championship. Rory bate su récord de birdies en el circuito
articles.summary: El 'León de Barrika' se pone al frente del Abu Dhabi Championship. Rory bate su récord de birdies en el circuito
articles.body: Deportivamente, el DP World Tour no deja de ser un circuito con mucho potencial pese a que las finanzas no le cuadren y requiera para subsistir de la ayuda del PGA Tour. La prueba la tenemos en la espectacular segunda ronda del Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, con movimientos muy interesantes por parte de varias de las estrellas que se han reunido esta semana Yas Links. El campo estaba asequible y esto ha permitido que los escasos espectadores que se han dado cita en el recorrido de la capital de Emiratos Árabes disfrutasen de un buen espectáculo. Jon Rahm ha seguido jugando sólido y su vuelta de 67 le permite escalar hasta el coliderato con 132 golpes en el acumulado. Comparte el primer puesto de la clasificación con su gran amigo Tyrrell Hatton, que tiró 65 en el día, y con Francesco Laporta, que con su 70 se quedó muy lejos de su 62 inicial. Tras ellos hay un grupo que comanda Rory McIlroy, que fue el hombre del día con su ronda de 63. Los 64 de David Puig (134), los 66 de Manuel Elvira (135) y los 65 de su hermano Nacho (138) los deja en buena situación de cara al fin de semana. Algo más retirado está el líder de la Race to Dubai, Eugenio Chacarra (141). Tras un primer día libre de bogeys, ‘Rahmbo’ materializó tres este viernes, pero lo contrarrestó con ocho birdies, cinco de ellos en los primeros nueve hoyos. El vasco estuvo en general bien en todas las facetas de su juego e incluso se mostró resolutivo cuando cometió errores. No llegó a estar tan ordenado como en la jornada inaugural y en Yas Links, donde ganar al campo es la tónica general, será imperativo seguir haciendo rondas bajas para ganar; quien ‘pinche’ uno de los dos días del fin de semana se puede despedir del triunfo. Los 71 golpes de Eugenio Chacarra no le han permitido avanzar en la clasificación. Lo cierto es que el comienzo del día para el madrileño fue soberbio, con cuatro birdies de tirón y un rendimiento increíble en el putt que no perduró. Se le escapó un inesperado bogey en el hoyo 5, pero en el 7 volvía a poner el -4 en su tarjeta y así cerró el primer tramo del recorrido. Llegaron los segundos nueve hoyos, en los que se lució el jueves, pero aquí los pequeños errores el español los pagó con dos bogeys y en el 14 firmó un doble bogey tras encadenar varios fallos, y eso que su salida había sido simplemente perfecta. Pese a jugar los cuatro hoyos finales bastante bien, no rascó ningún birdie más. Tras firmar su 71, Eugenio fue autocrítico: "Necesitaba un inicio fuerte, un arranque rápido, y lo tuve. No pude mantenerlo y jugar bien desde ese bogey en el 5. Jugué hoyos irregulares, y eso es lo que obtienes cuando no juegas buen golf. No golpeé bien [la bola], cometí errores graves, la puse en lugares equivocados, pateé fatal. Así que, sí, necesito mejorar; es solo golf. Evidentemente, no estar confiado con el driver me hace no confiar en muchos golpes desde el tee. Y luego pateeé realmente mal hoy", explicó Chacarra. El madrileño, agregó: "Solo es cuestión de trabajar más y mejorar. Evidentemente, aún no soy lo suficientemente bueno. Todo puede cambiar. Necesito otro arranque rápido mañana. Voy a ir a trabajar esta tarde y hablar con el equipo para ver por qué pasó eso. Con suerte, podremos arreglar las cosas para el fin de semana". Por otro lado McIlroy, que ha quedado segundo en el torneo en dos ocasiones y tercero la asombrosa cifra de seis veces, pero aún no ha saboreado la victoria en la capital de Emiratos, logró su mejor marca de birdies en una sola ronda en el DP World Tour: firmó 11, lo que le permitió alcanzar el 11 bajo par en su acumulado.

articles.title: Patriots’ TreVeyon Henderson reveals hospitalization after mystery medical emergency
articles.summary: Despite extensive medical testing, the second-year running back says the cause of his symptoms remains "unknown and unexplainable."
articles.body:
New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson , who has not played since Oct. 22 , says he was recently hospitalized for several days after experiencing an unexpected medical emergency involving unexplained neurological symptoms.

Henderson addressed his condition in a statement shared on Friday, saying he underwent extensive medical testing and evaluation while in the hospital.

"While the results of my comprehensive medical testing have come back positive and reassuring, the cause of this remains unknown and unexplainable," Henderson said.

Henderson said the symptoms have affected his strength, coordination, and some physical functions.

He plans to continue working with specialists and physical therapists as he focuses on his recovery.

"I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health," Henderson said. "My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priorities."

Henderson also thanked his wife, family and loved ones, the New England Patriots organization, his agent, medical team and teammates for their support.

He also leaned on his faith, referencing Romans 8:28, and thanked those who have offered prayers and encouragement during his recovery.

Henderson and his wife are asking for continued prayers and privacy.

"We respectfully ask for continued prayers and privacy as we focus on my health and recovery," Henderson said.

Henderson did not provide a timeline for a return.

He didn't play in Week 8 against the Miami Dolphins and has been ruled out for Week 9's game against the Green Bay Packers.

articles.standfirst: El norirlandés tenía claro que LIV 2.0 no saldría adelante
articles.summary: El norirlandés reconoce que
articles.body: LIV Golf ya es historia, ha comenzado oficialmente su proceso de disolución y BC Partners, el fondo de inversión que iba a poner 300 millones de dólares para relanzar el circuito, descartó el proyecto al comprobar la falta de apoyo por parte de los jugadores. El faraónico proyecto que puso en marcha el Fondo de Inversión Pública de Arabia Saudí (PIF) no ha pasado de los cinco años de vida y, en esencia, para lo que ha servido es para que se incrementen los premios de los jugadores, el PGA Tour se fortalezca con la entrada de un potente inversor, y Rory McIlroy y Tiger Woods monten un negocio de golf indoor. Lo de globalizar el golf de élite no pasará de los esfuerzos que hace el DP World Tour por estar en la mayoría de mercados. Que LIV Golf tal como se conocía ya estaba muerto es algo que ya se sabía, pero hasta ayer que fue la vista ante el tribunal de quiebras se albergaba una pequeña esperanza de que LIV 2.0 tirara hacia adelante. El proyecto se fue al traste y la frase más certera al respecto la ha dejado Rory McIlroy en todays-golfer.com. En una charla con el periodista Ben Parsons, el norirlandés ha dicho: "Si no pudieron hacer que funcionaran los 6.000 millones de dólares, nunca iban a hacer que funcionara con 300 millones". Esta semana el campeón del Masters lanzaba una broma con mensaje al decir que ya le hubiera gustado a Arnold Palmer que en su época hubiera surgido un LIV Golf para que se incrementara el dinero de los premios de forma desproporcionada. También comentó lo que tantos piensan, y es que se comenzó a construir la casa por el tejado: "LIV probablemente tenía una buena idea a medias, pero la ejecutaron bastante mal. Tenían mucho capital, pero creo que gran parte de ese capital se desperdició de alguna manera, y creo que podrían haber utilizado ese dinero de forma mucho más estratégica. Podrían haberse asociado con algunos de los organismos rectores del deporte. Sin duda, podrían haber hecho mejores cosas con él, en lugar de simplemente enriquecer a los profesionales del circuito que ya ganaban mucho dinero".
